### Parasite material

S. mansoni (NMRI strain) eggs were isolated from livers collected from experimentally infected mice perfused 40 days post-infection. All animal-regulated procedures, including the experimental mouse infections at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, were conducted under Home Office Project Licence No. P77E8A062 held by GR. All the protocols were presented and approved by the Animal Welfare and Ethical Review Body (AWERB) of the Wellcome Sanger Institute. The AWERB is constituted as required by the UK Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986 Amendment Regulations 2012.

### Nuclei count

S. mansoni eggs isolated from infected mouse livers were hatched under light in freshwater (Mann et al., 2010), and the miracidia collected within 4 hr of hatching. The sample was put on ice for an hour to sink and concentrate the larvae, and all but 1 ml of the water was removed. One ml of 8% paraformaldehyde (4% final PFA concentration) was added to fix the miracidia for 30 min at room temperature. The larvae were rinsed in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS)/Tween (0.1%) and mounted in DAPI Fluoromount for confocal imaging. The whole mounts were imaged on a Leica Sp8 using a ×40 objective with the pinhole set to 1 AU, and a 30–50% overlap between Z slices. The z-stacks were imported into ImageJ, and each nucleus was manually segmented and counted using the plugin TrakEM2 (Cardona et al., 2012).

### Single-cell tissue dissociation

S. mansoni miracidia for single-cell dissociation were collected as described above. Eggs isolated from mouse livers were hatched in nuclease-free water (NFW) and collected within 4 hr of hatching. Two samples of miracidia were collected; sample 1 contained approximately ~8250 individuals, and sample 2–11,700. The samples (live miracidia in NFW in Low Protein Binding 15 ml Falcon Tubes [cat# 30122216]) were placed on ice for an hour to sink and concentrate the larvae, and all but 20 μl of water was then removed.

Three hundred µl of digestion buffer (2.5 µl of 0.5 M Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) in 300 µl of Hank’s Buffered Salt Solution without Ca2+ and Mg2+ [HBSS−/−]) was added to the larvae. We reconstituted 250 mg of the enzyme Native Bacillus licheniformis Protease (NATE-0633, Creative Enzymes) (Adam et al., 2017) in 2.5 ml of HBSS−/− (to give a stock concentration of 100 mg/ml) and added 200 µl of this stock to the larvae in buffer (final enzyme concentration = 40 mg/ml). The samples were kept on ice for 45 min and pipetted gently ~20 times every 5 min. Two hundred µl of 25% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in 1× HBSS−/− was added to the sample to quench the enzyme, and 10 ml of ice-cold PBS+/+ was added to bring the BSA to ~0.5%. The samples were centrifuged at 350 × g for 5 min at 4°C, and all but 20 µl of the supernatant was removed. We reconstituted 5 mg of the enzyme Liberase (Thermolysin Medium) Research Grade (LIBTM-RO Roche) in 2 ml of PBS (to give a stock concentration of 2.5 mg/ml) and added 100 µl of this stock to the sample (final enzyme concentration = 2.08 mg/ml). The samples were incubated at room temperature for 15 min, pipetting gently ~10 times every 5 min. The suspension was passed through 60 and 30 µm cell strainers (Falcon) and resuspended in 5 ml of cold 1× PBS supplemented with 0.5% BSA. The samples were centrifuged at 350 × g for 10 min at 4°C, and all but 700 µl of the supernatant was removed.

Sample 1 cell suspension was sorted; 200 µl was used for a no-stain control for autofluorescence during cell counting and sorting. The remaining 500 µl of cell suspension was stained with 1 μg/ml of propidium iodide (PI; Sigma P4864) to label dead/dying cells. Sample 1 was sorted into an eppendorf tube using the BD Influx cell sorter (Becton Dickinson, NJ) by enriching for PI negative cells (i.e. live cells). It took ~3 hr from the beginning of the enzymatic digestion to generating single-cell suspensions ready for library preparation on the 10X Genomics Chromium platform. Sample 2 cell suspension was not sorted.

### 10X Genomics library preparation and sequencing

The 10X Genomics protocol (‘Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kits v3.1 User Guide’ available from https://assets.ctfassets.net/an68im79xiti/1eX2FPdpeCgnCJtw4fj9Hx/7cb84edaa9eca04b607f9193162994de/CG000204_ChromiumNextGEMSingleCell3_v3.1_Rev_D.pdf) was followed to create gel in emulsion beads (GEMs) containing single cells, hydrogel beads and reagents for reverse transcription, perform barcoded cDNA synthesis, and produce sequencing libraries from pooled cDNAs. The concentration of single-cell suspensions was approximately 119 cells/μl (sample 1) and 122 cells/μl (sample 2), as estimated by flow cytometry-based counting (Beckman Coulter Cytoflex S). We concentrated both samples to 732 cells/μl. We loaded two aliquots of sample 1 and two of sample 2 into four 10X reactions according to the 10X protocol (Chromium Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kits v3.1), intending to capture approximately 10,000 cells per reaction.

Library construction (following GEM breakage) using 10X reagents following the ‘Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kits v3.1 User Guide’. The four libraries were sequenced on one lane of Illumina Novaseq XP (28 bp read 1, 90 bp read 2, 10 bp index 1, 10 bp index 2). All raw sequence data are deposited in the ENA under study accession PRJEB45615.

### Mapping and quantification of single-cell RNA-seq

We mapped the single-cell RNA-seq data to version 10 of the S. mansoni reference genome (Buddenborg et al., 2021 and WormBase ParaSite Howe et al., 2016; Howe et al., 2017) using 10X Genomics Cell Ranger (version 6.0.1) (Zheng et al., 2017). Before mapping, exon 8 was removed from Smp_323380 and the 3′ end was trimmed from Smp_337410 to reduce erroneous mapping to the W chromosome from Z gametologs. The Cell Ranger implementation of EmptyDrops (Lun et al., 2019) was used to detect cells and empty droplets. Across the four samples, on average 63.88% of the reads mapped confidently to the transcriptome (63.4% for sorted, 64.35% for unsorted), and an average 83.65% of reads were associated with a cell. There were an average of 118,395 reads per cell. Across the four samples, we captured an estimated 33,319 cells: 8815 and 24,504 cells from sorted and unsorted samples, respectively. The median gene count was 1660, and the median UMI count was 5343. Following QC, 20,478 cells remained for onward analysis.

### QC and clustering using Seurat

The four samples were imported into Seurat (version 4.3.0) (Hao et al., 2021) using R (version 4.1.3) in RStudio (version 1.4.1106) for QC, clustering, and marker gene identification. The four samples were initially processed separately. Cells with less than 200 genes expressed and genes in less than three cells were removed. QC metrics, including gene distribution and UMI counts per cell, were inspected visually and used to select QC cut-offs. Following a preliminary analysis without further cell filtering, cells with fewer than 500 UMIs were removed, and a maximum mitochondrial threshold of 5% was applied. This was based on data distribution, best practices from the authors of the software, and other similar studies; here, we were aiming to remove low-quality cells while being relatively permissive as there may be cell types in these data outside of standard filtering parameters. Based on existing knowledge of this larva, we were expecting both multinucleate and anucleate cell type(s) as well as single-nuclei cells (Pan, 1980). The data were normalised, scaled (regressing for mitochondrial gene percentage), and variable genes were identified for clustering following Seurat guidelines. Throughout the analysis of these data, several tools were used to select the optimal number of PCs to use: Seurat’s ElbowPlot and JackStraw, and molecular cross-validation (https://github.com/constantAmateur/MCVR/blob/master/code.R; Young, 2022), and Seurat’s clustree tool was used to assess the stability of clusters with increasing resolution. We employed DoubletFinder (McGinnis et al., 2019) to identify multiplets, which can lead to spurious signals. The estimated doublet rate was calculated based on 10X loading guidelines and adjusted for our sample concentrations; we estimated multiplet rates at 8% for sorted samples and 52.8% for unsorted samples. We used paramSweep, as recommended, to identify the optimum parameters for each sample in our data and removed cells classified as multiplets. DoubletFinder removed 299 and 303 cells from the two sorted samples, and 6069 and 5496 cells from the two unsorted samples.

We then combined the two sorted samples and the two unsorted samples (producing one sorted object and one unsorted object). We used SCTransform to normalise and scale these two objects (with regression for mitochondrial percentage and sample ID). Seurat’s IntegrateData function was then used to integrate the sorted and unsorted samples (with normalization.method = "SCT"). This resulted in 20,478 cells passing all the QC filters and going onto the primary analysis, 3849 and 3962 from the sorted samples and 6702 and 5965 from the unsorted samples.

Following integration, principal component analysis (PCA) was run for up to 100 PCs. The data were explored using a range of PCs and resolutions and using the tools listed above, 55 PCs and a resolution of 1 were selected for the analysis. We manually segmented out the cells in the Neuron 3 cluster based on clear differences in gene expression. Top markers were identified using Seurat’s FindAllMarkers (min.pct = 0.0, logfc.threshold = 0.0, test.use = "roc") as recommended by Seurat best practices (https://satijalab.org/seurat/) to capture subtle differences in gene expression, and were sorted by AUC. We used the identity and expression of top marker genes (as identified by AUC), along with previously published cell- and tissue-type marker gene expression, to determine the identity of the cell clusters. To link gene description and chromosome locations to gene IDs, the GFF for the latest publicly available genome version was downloaded from WBPS (WBPS18 release, Howe et al., 2016; Howe et al., 2017).

### Sex-effect analysis

To investigate sex effects on the single-cell transcriptome, the cells were categorised as W+ or W− (an approximation of female and male cells, respectively, as males lack WSR genes). As ground-truth data were absent, the % of reads mapping to ZSR and WSR was calculated using Seurat’s PercentageFeatureSet. Cells with 0.2% or more reads mapping to the WSR were classified as W+, and the remaining cells were classified as W−. The 0.2% threshold was selected (Figure 5—figure supplement 4) to avoid classifying ZZ cells with a few transcripts erroneously mapping to a gene on the WSR as W+. This produced 8702 cells labelled as W+, and 11,776 cells labelled as W−.

### SAM algorithm

The count data from the QC-filtered Seurat analysis were exported for SAM (v1.0.1) analysis. For each SAM analysis, the raw count data were imported as a SAM object, standard preprocessing done (using default SAM parameters), and the SAM algorithm (Tarashansky et al., 2019) run. For further analysis, the object was converted into a Scanpy (v 1.8.2) (Wolf et al., 2018) object, top markers extracted, and metadata from the Seurat analysis were attached. This method was repeated on the Neuron 1 cluster alone, to better understand the transcriptome heterogeneity.

### RNA velocity

All four miracidia samples and the raw data from the mother sporocyst (Diaz Soria et al., 2024) were pseudo-mapped using kallisto bustools (v 0.27.3) Melsted et al., 2021 using the lamanno workflow to the version 10 S. mansoni genome (WBPS18 release Howe et al., 2016; Howe et al., 2017, with the same amendments as listed above). The filtered spliced and unspliced matrices for each sample individually were imported to R. DropletUtils (v 1.20.0) (Lun et al., 2019) and BUSpaRse (v 1.14.1) (Moses, 2023) were used to process and QC the matrices, and filter out cells and genes with few reads. The matrices were then converted to Seurat objects and further filtered so only cells with the cell barcodes that passed QC filtering in the primary Seurat analysis were retained. The metadata and raw counts of the unspliced and spliced reads following filtering were exported as CSV files. The same method was performed on the mother sporocyst samples, which were combined before exporting. For the joint analyses of miracidia and sporocyst cells, the combined sporocyst Seurat object was merged with each of the four miracidia samples separately (due to the mismatch in sample size and batch effect between sorted and unsorted samples) and all were exported.

The CSV files containing spliced and unspliced reads, together with sample metadata were combined to make an AnnData object using Scanpy (v 1.8.2, Python v 3.8.5) (Wolf et al., 2018). Using scvelo (v 0.2.4) (Bergen et al., 2020), the standard parameters were used to filter and normalise the data, compute moments, and recover dynamics. Velocity was calculated using the dynamical mode. Following PCA, a UMAP was generated (n_neighbors = 10, n_pcs = 40) and Leiden clustering was added (resolution = 0.8). The top-ranked dynamical genes for each cluster and known genes of interest were plotted. This was performed for each of the four miracidia samples combined with the sporocyst samples, with and without the use of combat for batch correction. As the sporocyst samples were also sorted, we used the sorted miracidia samples to reduce technical effects.

To focus on the stem/germinal and tegument clusters, the same method as above was used after subsetting the data in Seurat to contain only cells from the clusters Stem/germinal, Tegument 1, and Tegument 2 in the sporocyst samples, and only Stem A–G and Tegument clusters from the miracidia clusters.

We present the stem and tegument cells from the sporocyst stage merged with sample 1 (sorted). The equivalent results from sporocysts merged with sample 4 of the miracidia and results with all cells from those two conditions are available in the supplementary data (Figure 6—figure supplements 4–6).

### EdU-staining experiment

Miracidia were collected as described above for 2 hr. As miracidia continually hatched over this time period, they ranged from 0 to 2 hr post-hatching. The miracidia were collected and split into two samples: one for EdU labelling and the second for a negative control (miracidia in water without EdU). Sample one was pulsed with 500 µM EdU in water for 4 hr. Sample two was kept in water for 4 hr. Both samples were fixed in 4% PFA for 30 min at room temperature. EdU incorporation was detected by click reaction with 25 µM Alexa Fluor488 Azide conjugates (Invitrogen) for 30 min. As a positive control, we pulsed freshly transformed mother sporocysts in EdU for 3 days (Wang et al., 2013). Three biological replicates were carried out, with 20 miracidia and 20 mother sporocysts per treatment examined for each replicate.

### Plate-based scRNAseq analysis of individually isolated cells

A sample of thousands of miracidia was dissociated into a single-cell suspension using the dissociation protocol described above. Individual gland cells, ciliary plates, and unknown cells were picked up one at time using an EZ Grip transfer pipette set to aspirate a 3-µl volume (Research Instruments Ltd 7-72-2800). Each cell was placed in a well of a 96-well plate containing a lysis buffer (NEBNext Cell Lysis Buffer, E6428). cDNA was generated using the NEB low input RNA kit (E6420). DNA library construction was carried out using the NEBNext Ultra II FS DNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (E7805). The libraries were sequenced on one lane of NovaSeq SP. The reads from the 96 samples were pseudoaligned to the version 10 S. mansoni genome (WBPS18 release Howe et al., 2016; Howe et al., 2017, with the same amendments as listed above using kallisto (v 0.44.0) Bray et al., 2016). These were imported into R (v4.3.1) and the metadata were inspected, after which only samples coming from a single cell with a minimum of 20% reads pseudoaligned were retained (n = 76). The samples were then processed using sleuth (v0.30.1) Pimentel et al., 2017 following guidance from sleuth tutorials, including the steps for normalising, fitting error models, and differential analysis. Differential analysis was used to identify significant genes between the cell types, which were visualised, along with known genes of interest, using sleuth’s heatmap function. Furthermore, the kallisto outputs were used to calculate the top 200 genes by median TPM of the two key cell types of interest, ciliary plates and gland cells, and these were used for GO term analysis following the method described below.

### In situ hybridisation

Miracidia collected as described above within 4 hr of hatching were fixed in 4% PFA in 2 μm filtered PBSTw (1× PBS + 0.1% Tween) at room temperature for 30 min on a rocker. The larvae were transferred to incubation baskets (Intavis, 35 µm mesh) in a 24-well plate, rinsed 3 × 5 min in PBSTw, and incubated in 5 μg/ml Proteinase K (Invitrogen) in 1× PBSTw for 5 min at room temperature. They were post-fixed in 4% Formaldehyde in PBSTx for 10 min at room temperature and then rinsed in PBSTw for 10 min. From this point on, the in situ hybridisation experiments followed the protocol described by Choi et al., 2016 and developed for wholemount nematode larvae. We carried out fluorescent in situ hybridisation on 27 cell-type marker genes. Probes, buffers, and hairpins for third-generation in situ hybridisation chain reaction experiments were purchased from Molecular Instruments (Los Angeles, California, USA) (Choi et al., 2018). Molecular Instruments designed probes against the sequences on WormBase ParaSite (WBPS version 18, WS271, Howe et al., 2017; Supplementary file 1R). We subsequently labelled some larvae with phalloidin by adding 1 µl phalloidin to 1 ml 5× SSCT (Sodium Chloride and Sodium Citrate buffer [Invitrogen AM9763] + 0.1% Tween) (for an hour at room temperature in the dark, then rinsing 6 × 30 min in SSCT, incubating overnight at 4°C in DAPI fluoromount-G (Southern Biotech) and then mounting and imaging on a confocal laser microscope (Leica Sp8)). We carried out at more than three in situ hybridisation experiments for each marker gene we validated (each experiment was a biological replicate). From each experiment, we imaged (by confocal microscopy) 10 miracidia (technical replicates) per marker gene experiment. To count the number of cells belonging to each tissue type we imported confocal z-stacks of tissue marker gene expression (Figure 8—videos 1–3) into ImageJ, and using the plugin TrakEM2 (Cardona et al., 2012), manually segmented each nucleus that was expressing, and was surrounded, by the transcripts.

### Opsin phylogeny

Amino acid sequences for selected metazoan opsin proteins were obtained from the GenBank database and aligned using the – auto mode of MAFFT v7.450 (Katoh and Standley, 2013), then trimmed using trimAl v1.4.rev22 (Capella-Gutiérrez et al., 2009) to remove alignment columns with more than 50% gap characters ensuring at least 50% of alignment columns were maintained in the final alignment. Phylogenetic analysis of this alignment was performed using RaxML v8.2.12 (Stamatakis, 2014). The best-fitting empirical amino acid substitution model was identified as maximising the log-likelihood of the data under a model incorporating gamma-distributed variation in substitution rates across sites, and this optimal model (Le Gascuel,LG) was used for subsequent inference. The maximum-likelihood tree and branch lengths were identified as the highest likelihood from 25 independent searches starting from different random starting tree topologies, and support for partitions on this tree was estimated using 1000 bootstrap replicates of resampling alignment positions with replacement, using the fast bootstrap (−x) algorithm implemented in RaxML.

### Protein–protein interaction analysis

Protein interactions were predicted using the online search tool STRING https://www.string-db.org/; V 11; Szklarczyk et al., 2019 for the following well-defined cell clusters: Neurons 3–5, ciliary plates, protonephridia, Parenchyma 1 and 2, tegument, and the two main stem cell populations, Delta/Phi and Kappa. Protein sequences for the top 100 marker genes for each cell cluster were collected from WormBase ParaSite. The protein sequences were entered as a multiple protein search. Default settings were used to predict interactions with either a minimum interaction (confidence) score of 0.4 or 0.7, corresponding to a medium or high level of confidence.

### GO enrichment analysis

Each cluster’s list of marker genes was filtered to focus on specific cluster markers. Genes were retained for analysis if they had a minimum AUC score of 0.7. To compare the functional enrichment in Stem 1 vs Stem 2, Stem A was combined with Stem B and Stem C was combined with Stem D, and the differentially expressed markers were identified using Seurat’s FindMarkers. These markers were filtered (with adjusted p-values <0.001) and used as the basis for GO enrichment analysis in the Delta/Phi and Kappa stem clusters. TopGO (version 2.46.0) (Alexa and Rahnenfuhrer, 2023) was used in R with the weight01 method to identify enriched GO terms. Node size was set to a minimum of five terms, and analysis was run for each cluster on the Biological Process and Molecular Function categories. Fisher’s exact test was used to assess the statistical significance of overrepresented terms, with an FDR threshold set <0.05. The same method was used to identify overrepresented terms in the WSR genes, ZSR genes, and WSR together with ZSR genes for the BP, MF, and Cellular Component categories.

Beyond generating lists of genes that are differentially expressed in different cell types, the authors validated many of the cluster-defining genes using in situ hybridization chain reaction. In addition to providing the field with markers for many of the cell types in the parasite at this stage, the authors use these markers to count the total number of various cell types in the organism. Because the authors realized that their cell isolation protocols were biasing the cell types they were sequencing, they applied a second method to help them recover additional cell types.

Schistosomes have ZW sex chromosomes and the authors make the interesting observation that the stem cells at this stage are already expressing sex (i.e. W)-specific genes.

Comments on revised version:

The manuscript has been improved after revisions. The methods, data and analyses broadly support the claims with only minor weaknesses.

claims.claim: The transcriptomes of the tegumental cells show a predicted network of genes involved in protein folding, export, and translocation.
claims.source: Between all the ciliary plates sit the ridges of the tegumental cells. The ridges connect to the cell bodies beneath the body wall musculature, and their transcriptomes show a predicted network of genes involved in protein folding, export, and translocation.
claims.evidence: This is based on STRING analysis of tegument marker genes.

claims.claim: Ultrastructural studies have observed abundant RER, ribosomes, Golgi apparatus, and complex carbohydrates in tegumental cell bodies, suggesting they are active in producing exportable proteins.
claims.source: This is consistent with ultrastructural studies that have observed abundant RER, ribosomes, Golgi apparatus, and complex carbohydrates in these cell bodies, suggesting they are active in producing exportable proteins (Meuleman et al., 1978; Pan, 1980).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Meuleman et al., 1978; Pan, 1980.

claims.claim: Large numbers of membrane-bound vesicles were observed in tegumental cells and thought to become part of the new tegument membrane (syncytium) that rapidly forms around the mother sporocyst during the early stages of transformation.
claims.source: Large numbers of membrane-bound vesicles were also observed and thought to become part of the new tegument membrane (syncytium) that rapidly forms around the mother sporocyst during the early stages of transformation, protecting the mother sporocyst from attack by the snails' amoebocytes (Pan, 1980).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pan, 1980.

claims.claim: The RNA velocity analysis has revealed dynamic genes that may be crucial in the maturation of the tegument cells across the miracidium to sporocyst life cycle transition.
claims.source: The RNA velocity analysis has revealed dynamic genes that may be crucial in the maturation of the tegument cells across this life cycle transition, and in turn, for evasion of host defences and parasite survival.
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA velocity analysis.

claims.claim: Many of the molecular regulators and markers of adult tegument biogenesis are expressed in the miracidia and sporocyst stem and tegument cells, indicating that there is a conserved molecular programme for the development of the syncytial tegument.
claims.source: Many of the molecular regulators and markers of adult tegument biogenesis (Collins et al., 2016; Wendt et al., 2018; Wendt et al., 2022) are expressed in the miracidia and sporocyst stem and tegument cells, indicating that there is a conserved molecular programme for the development of the syncytial tegument in the mother sporocyst and its maintenance in the adult worm.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of gene expression across life stages, with citations to Collins et al., 2016; Wendt et al., 2018; Wendt et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The transcriptomes of the two stem populations in the miracidium suggest they are in different activation states.
claims.source: The transcriptomes of the two stem populations in the miracidium suggest they are in different activation states.
claims.evidence: This is based on GO analysis and marker gene expression.

claims.claim: This finding aligns with the discovery of two stem cell populations in the mother sporocyst that have different proliferation kinetics.
claims.source: This finding aligns with the discovery of two stem cell populations in the mother sporocyst that have different proliferation kinetics (Wang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The pre-activated state of Delta/Phi stem cells in the miracidia may signify that they are the first population to proliferate once the miracidium transforms into the mother sporocyst inside the snail.
claims.source: The pre-activated state of Delta/Phi stem cells in the miracidia may signify that they are the first population to proliferate once the miracidium transforms into the mother sporocyst inside the snail.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the observed activation state.

claims.claim: The finding that eled and many of the germline-specific regulatory programme components are expressed in some miracidia Kappa cells suggests that when a miracidium hatches, the cells that will contribute to the germline may already be segregated.
claims.source: The finding that eled, and many of the germline-specific regulatory programme components, are expressed in some miracidia Kappa cells suggests that when a miracidium hatches, the cells that will contribute to the germline may already be segregated and the molecular regulatory programme that differentiates somatic (Delta/Phi) and germ cell (Kappa) lineages is present.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on expression of germline-specific genes.

claims.claim: The presence of spliced-only copies of the germline defining genes eled and boule could suggest that they are maternal transcripts that have been restricted to the primordial germ cells during embryogenesis.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the presence of spliced-only copies of the germline defining genes eled and boule could suggest that they are maternal transcripts that have been restricted to the primordial germ cells during embryogenesis, as is the case in Zebrafish embryos (Fishman et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of spliced-only transcripts, with citation to Fishman et al., 2023.

claims.claim: An alternative explanation for the presence of spliced-only copies of eled and boule is that unspliced transcripts exist but their abundance was below the threshold for detection.
claims.source: An alternative explanation is that unspliced transcripts exist for these lowly expressed genes but their abundance was below our threshold for detection.
claims.evidence: This is an alternative explanation for the observation.

claims.claim: The degree of transcriptomic sexual difference was most evident in the Delta/Phi and Kappa stem cell clusters, with no distinct clustering by sex observed in other cell clusters.
claims.source: This degree of transcriptomic sexual difference was most evident in the Delta/Phi and Kappa stem cell clusters, with no distinct clustering by sex observed in other cell clusters.
claims.evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of cells with and without sex chromosome genes.

claims.claim: Incomplete gene dosage compensation in the miracidium could explain the sex-biased clustering of stem cells.
claims.source: This could be explained by incomplete gene dosage compensation in the miracidium.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed sex-biased clustering.

claims.claim: Tissue-specific variation could add a further dimension to the role of dosage compensation in schistosomes.
claims.source: Following investigations of differences in gene dosage compensation across developmental stages using bulk RNA-seq (Picard et al., 2019), our study suggests tissue-specific variation could add a further dimension to the role of dosage compensation in schistosomes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed tissue-specific differences in sex-biased gene expression, with citation to Picard et al., 2019.

claims.claim: A similar phenomenon of tissue-specific dosage compensation has been described in mouse embryonic stem cells and in Drosophila.
claims.source: A similar phenomenon has been described in mouse embryonic stem cells and in Drosophila, where a precise regulation of a gene-by-gene dosage compensation mechanism is critical to the proper development of specific tissues and organs, such as the wing and eye (Valsecchi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Valsecchi et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Sex differences in undifferentiated stem cells have not been reported in later stages of the schistosome life cycle.
claims.source: In contrast to the miracidium, sex differences in undifferentiated stem cells have not been reported in later stages of the schistosome life cycle (Wang et al., 2018; Diaz Soria et al., 2020; Wendt et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2018; Diaz Soria et al., 2020; Wendt et al., 2020.

claims.claim: It may not have been possible to detect sex differences in stem cells in earlier studies because scRNA-seq data were mapped onto older versions of the genome, where the sex chromosomes were not as well defined.
claims.source: In fact, it may not have been possible to detect these differences in earlier studies because scRNA-seq data were mapped onto older versions of the genome, where the sex chromosomes were not as well defined (Buddenborg et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about why sex differences were not detected in previous studies, with citation to Buddenborg et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The present study has benefited from a high level of coverage, enabling differences in stem cells to be more easily discerned.
claims.source: In addition to using an improved reference annotation, the present study has also benefited from a high level of coverage, enabling differences in stem cells to be more easily discerned.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the current study.

claims.claim: The current understanding of schistosome development is that differentiated somatic cells of the miracidium do not continue into the daughter sporocyst stage, the cercariae and beyond; it is the stem cells that persist and differentiate into the cell types of the subsequent life stages.
claims.source: The current understanding of schistosome development is that differentiated somatic cells of the miracidium do not continue into the daughter sporocyst stage, the cercariae and beyond; it is the stem cells that persist and differentiate into the cell types of the subsequent life stages (Wang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: All miracidium somatic cells are miracidium-only cells.
claims.source: In this respect, all miracidium somatic cells are miracidium-only cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the understanding that somatic cells do not persist beyond the miracidium stage.

claims.claim: The transcriptional signatures of miracidium somatic cells are similar to comparable tissue types at later stages.
claims.source: Our atlas shows that their transcriptional signatures are similar to comparable tissue types at later stages (Diaz Soria et al., 2020; Wendt et al., 2020; Diaz Soria et al., 2024)
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of gene expression across life stages, with citations to Diaz Soria et al., 2020; Wendt et al., 2020; Diaz Soria et al., 2024.

claims.claim: There may be conserved tissue-specific molecular developmental programmes that are deployed multiple times during the complex life cycle.
claims.source: and that there may be conserved tissue-specific molecular developmental programmes that are deployed multiple times during the complex life cycle.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of transcriptional signatures across life stages.

results.result: The manuscript provides background information on Schistosoma mansoni, its life cycle, and the disease burden of schistosomiasis. The miracidium is described as the first larval stage that infects freshwater snails and transforms into a mother sporocyst, which generates daughter sporocysts and cercariae. Schistosomiasis causes 1.0–2.6 million DALYs and over 11,000 deaths annually.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C5, C21-C27) are well-established facts about S. mansoni biology and schistosomiasis epidemiology, supported by citations to WHO, IHME, and peer-reviewed literature. They provide essential context for the study but are not novel findings.

results.result: The miracidium is composed of approximately 365 cells (median=365, range 342-377 across three larvae). Single-cell RNA-seq generated data from 20,478 cells that passed quality control, with a median of 858 genes and 1761 UMI counts per cell.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C35-C37 report direct measurements from the study. The cell count is based on manual segmentation of DAPI-stained nuclei (C6), and the scRNA-seq metrics (C35-C37) are standard quality control measures that are clearly reported. These provide the foundational data for the atlas.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing identified 19 transcriptionally distinct cell clusters in the miracidium, comprising two muscle clusters (3934 cells), five neuronal clusters (3255 cells), one ciliary plate cluster (40 cells), one tegumental cluster (366 cells), one protonephridial cluster (539 cells), two parenchymal clusters (1698 cells), and seven stem cell clusters (10,686 cells).
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C38-C44 describe the primary clustering results from the scRNA-seq analysis. The identification of 19 clusters is supported by the UMAP visualization (Figure 1C) and marker gene expression (Figure 1D). The cell counts for each cluster are directly reported from the Seurat analysis. This is a core finding of the study.

results.result: In situ hybridization revealed that 93% of miracidium cells are somatic (57% neural, 19% muscle, 13% epidermal/tegument, 2% parenchyma, 2% protonephridia) and 7% are stem cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C14 report the cellular composition of the miracidium based on in situ hybridization and cell counting. These percentages are calculated from counts of marker-positive cells relative to the total ~365 cells per larva. The data are supported by multiple ISH experiments (Figures 2-5) with clear quantification. This is a major finding that defines the cellular architecture of the miracidium.

results.result: Two muscle clusters were identified based on expression of paramyosin, troponin t, and titin. ISH identified 74 paramyosin-positive nuclei (~19% of cells), comprising 28 circular muscle nuclei, 33 longitudinal muscle nuclei, and 13 nuclei in an anterior unilateral cluster. Muscle cluster 1 (circular) expresses Kunitz-type protease inhibitor and Wnt-11-1 at the posterior pole, while Notum is expressed anteriorly. Muscle cluster 2 (longitudinal) expresses calcium-activated potassium channel and MyoD.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C57 describe the muscle cell populations with detailed spatial and molecular characterization. The identification is based on known muscle markers (C45, citations provided), ISH with cell counting (C46-C51, Figure 2B-C), and differential marker expression (C52-C57, Figure 2D-F). The data clearly distinguish circular and longitudinal muscle subtypes with distinct transcriptional profiles and spatial organization.

results.result: Five neural clusters were identified expressing complexin, prohormone convertase 2, and Smp_068500. Complexin was expressed in at least 209 nuclei (57% of cells), with 129 in the brain and 80 peripheral. Neuron 1 (1470 cells) contains subpopulations expressing neuropeptide precursors (PWamide, Neuropeptide F, Neuropeptide Y) and putative photoreceptor cells expressing opsins. Neurons 2-5 were characterized by specific markers including NPP-43, NPP-26, Smp_319480 (putative mTORC1), and an EF-hand domain protein, with distinct spatial localizations.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C80 comprehensively characterize the neural cell populations. The five clusters are identified by marker expression (C58, Figure 3A), with cell counts from ISH (C59-C61, Figure 3B). Subclustering of Neuron 1 (C62-C64) is supported by SAM analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Neurons 2-5 are validated by ISH with specific markers (C65-C80, Figure 3C-F, supplementary figures). The identification of polycystin genes (C76) and functional predictions are reasonable inferences from the data.

results.result: Plate-based single-cell RNA-seq of 37 manually selected gland cells revealed co-expression of neural markers (Complexin, 7B2) and muscle markers (Myosin light chain 1, Troponin t, Actin-2), as well as five venom antigen-like (VAL) genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 describe the transcriptome of penetration gland cells using an alternative scRNA-seq approach. The co-expression of neural and muscle markers (C82) and VAL genes (C83) is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6. This approach was necessary because gland cells were not captured in the 10X data (C148), and the findings are clearly supported by the plate-based data.

results.result: A cluster of 40 cells was identified as ciliary plates based on expression of 16-kDa calcium-binding protein (CaBP) and p25 alpha. ISH revealed expression in ciliary plates and in six previously undescribed submuscular cells that project to the exterior.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 identify the ciliary plate cluster and a novel submuscular cell type. The cluster identification is based on marker expression (C84, Figure 3A, citation to Wendt et al. 2020), and ISH confirms expression in ciliary plates and submuscular cells (C85-C86, Figure 3G). The discovery of the submuscular cells is a novel finding supported by clear imaging data.

results.result: A cluster of 366 cells was identified as tegumental based on expression of adult tegument markers including dynein light chain, DUF3421 domain protein, and MEG6. ISH showed 46 Meg6-positive cells with nuclei in the posterior two-thirds of the larva, with cytoplasmic protrusions forming epidermal ridges between ciliary plates.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C90 characterize the tegumental cell population. The cluster is identified by known tegument markers from adult worms (C87, citation to Wendt et al. 2020), with ISH validation showing spatial distribution and morphology (C89-C90, Figure 4C-D). The data clearly support the identification of these cells as tegumental precursors.

results.result: The protonephridial cluster (536 cells) expressed genes common to excretory systems including nephrin and odd-skipped-related. Eighty percent of cells expressed Smp_335600 (ShKT-domain protein), which was localized around six nuclei in a bilaterally symmetrical pattern along the s-shaped excretory tubules connecting anterior and posterior flame cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C95 characterize the protonephridial system. The cluster is identified by conserved excretory markers (C92, citation to Gąsiorowski et al. 2021) and a known protonephridia marker (C93, citation to Nanes Sarfati et al. 2021). ISH reveals the spatial organization of the excretory system (C94-C95, Figure 4E), consistent with known ultrastructure.

results.result: Two parenchyma clusters (1093 and 605 cells) were identified expressing markers similar to later developmental stages. A zinc transporter Slc39a7 (Smp_318890) was expressed in 7-9 cells with long cytoplasmic protrusions filling intercellular spaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C100 characterize the parenchymal cell populations. The clusters are identified by markers from later stages (C97, citations provided), with ISH showing spatial distribution and morphology (C99-C100, Figure 4B, F). The data support the identification of these cells as parenchyma, though the distinction between the two clusters is less clear from ISH alone.

results.result: Seven stem cell clusters (10,686 cells) were identified by expression of ago2-1. Stems A and B are Kappa-like (klf+, nanos-2+), while Stems C and D are Delta/Phi-like (nanos-2+, fgfrA+, fgfrB+, hesl+). The two populations are distinguished by sex-linked gene expression; when sex chromosome genes are removed, they collapse into single clusters. ISH showed 20-29 ago2-1+ cells (median 23, ~7% of cells), with 12-14 p53-1+ (Delta/Phi) and 8-9 UPPA+ (Kappa) cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C115 characterize the stem cell populations. The clusters are identified by known stem markers (C101, citations to Wang et al. 2013, 2018), with classification based on marker expression (C103-C104). The sex-based clustering is demonstrated by re-analysis after removing sex chromosome genes (C105-C106, Figure 5B). ISH validates the two main populations (C109-C115, Figure 5C-D). This is a major finding revealing sex-biased gene expression in stem cells.

results.result: Neurons represent the most diverse somatic cell types. Trajectory analysis indicates that one of the two main stem cell populations is the origin of the tegument lineage, while the other likely contains pluripotent cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C18 summarize key findings. Neuronal diversity (C15) is evident from five distinct clusters. The trajectory analysis (C16-C18) is based on RNA velocity analysis combining miracidia and sporocyst data (Figure 6), showing Delta/Phi stem cells progressing toward tegument (C17) and Kappa cells expressing germline markers (C18). These are well-supported inferences from the data.

results.result: Each of the two main stem cell populations shows sex-biased transcriptional signatures, suggesting cell-type-specific gene dosage compensation for sex chromosome-linked loci. Sex-linked gene dosage is not fully compensated in the miracidium, with tissue-specific variation.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20, C108, C181-C182 describe sex-biased gene expression in stem cells. The clustering by sex is clearly demonstrated (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), and the interpretation of incomplete dosage compensation (C108, C182) is a reasonable inference from the observed differences in ZSR gene expression between male and female cells. The tissue-specificity is supported by the observation that sex-biased clustering is most evident in stem cells (C181).

results.result: DNA replication does not take place in stem or somatic cells during the free-swimming miracidium stage, as shown by lack of EdU incorporation. Since stem cells start proliferating ~20 hr post-infection in the mother sporocyst, both stem cell populations pause cell division for at least 26 hr.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118 report the absence of cell division in the miracidium. The lack of EdU incorporation (C116, Figure 5—figure supplement 5) is clear experimental evidence. The inference about the pause in cell division (C118) is based on combining this observation with the timing of proliferation in sporocysts (C117, citation to Wang et al. 2013). This is a well-supported finding.

results.result: Many top markers for Delta/Phi and Kappa stem clusters are ribosomal proteins, forming networks enriched for translation and ribosome biogenesis. Six transcription factors are upregulated in Delta/Phi (lin-39, tiptop, hes-related, p53-1, Zfp-1, six-3-1), indicating a multipotent progenitor stage. GO analysis shows Delta/Phi genes are related to ribosome and translation (pre-activation markers), while Kappa genes are involved in transcription and metabolism (quiescent markers).
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C125 characterize the molecular states of the two stem populations. The enrichment of ribosomal proteins (C119-C120) is shown by STRING analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 6). Differential expression of transcription factors (C121) and metabolic genes (C123) is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 7A. The GO analysis (C124-C125) is supported by citations to studies on stem cell activation states. The interpretation of multipotency (C122) is a reasonable inference supported by citation.

results.result: The Delta/Phi stem population co-expresses three tegument/epidermal lineage-specific transcription factors (p53-1, zfp-1, six3-1), suggesting it is the origin of miracidia tegument cells and the source of new tegument in the mother sporocyst. RNA velocity analysis indicates progression of Delta/Phi stem cells toward miracidia tegument cells, with high-speed differentiation to sporocyst tegument. The miracidia tegument cluster may contain cells ranging from post-mitotic stem cell progeny to terminally differentiated cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C132 describe the tegument lineage trajectory. The co-expression of tegument-specific transcription factors (C126, citations provided) is shown in the scRNA-seq data. The RNA velocity analysis (C128-C129, Figure 6B-C) provides computational evidence for the developmental trajectory. The dynamics of p53-1 and zfp-1 expression (C131-C132, Figure 6D-E) support the progression model. This is a major finding linking stem cells to differentiated tegument.

results.result: The Kappa stem population expresses genes detected in germline stem cells and germ cells in intra-mammalian stages, including p53-2 (highly expressed and actively transcribed) and germline-specific regulatory genes (eled, onecut1, irx, akkn, boule). Together, these data suggest Delta/Phi is the origin of the tegumental lineage and contributes to extra-embryonic somatic tissues, while Kappa likely contains pluripotent cells that will contribute to cercariae development and the germline.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C138 characterize the Kappa population and propose its fate. The expression of germline markers (C133, C136, citations to Wang et al. 2018, Li et al. 2021) is shown in the scRNA-seq data and RNA velocity analysis (Figure 6F-G). The expression of p53-2 (C134-C135) is supported by RNA velocity and citation. The conclusions about lineage fates (C137-C138) are reasonable inferences from the combined expression and trajectory data, though they remain predictions requiring future validation.

results.result: Prior scRNA-seq studies have identified stem cell heterogeneity, classified differentiated cell types, and revealed key genes essential for parasite survival across the schistosome life cycle. Studies have been performed on mother sporocyst, schistosomulum, juvenile, and adult stages, but single-cell data for the miracidium larva was lacking prior to this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 provide literature context. These are accurate summaries of prior work, supported by appropriate citations. The identification of the gap in miracidium single-cell data (C32) justifies the current study. These are minor contextual claims.

results.result: The miracidium is a short-lived, non-feeding stage relying on internal energy stores. Eight major systems have been previously identified at the ultrastructural level: musculature, nervous, penetration gland cells, excretory, interstitial (parenchyma), stem/germinal cells, epithelial, and terebratorium.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 provide background on miracidium biology from prior ultrastructural studies, supported by citations to Pan 1980 and others. These are established facts that provide context for the molecular characterization in this study.

results.result: The miracidium, with its diversity of differentiated cells in relatively low numbers (~365 cells), makes a simple and tractable system for understanding schistosome cell biology. Compared to later stages (cercariae ~1600 cells, schistosomulum ~900 cells, adults tens of thousands), the miracidium is a simple stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C143 provide context and conclusions about the utility of the miracidium as a model system. The cell counts for later stages are supported by citations (C140, C142) or stated as unpublished data (C143). The conclusion about simplicity and tractability (C139) is a reasonable inference from the data presented.

results.result: Stem cells accounted for ~52% of scRNA-seq data despite comprising only 7% of cells in the larva, indicating preferential recovery. Ciliary plates were only found in sufficient numbers in unsorted samples. Preferential recovery may be due to differences in cell robustness to dissociation, sorting, and/or 10X GEM capture. There are clear benefits to including unsorted samples to discover cell type diversity.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C147 discuss technical aspects of the scRNA-seq approach. The overrepresentation of stem cells (C144) is documented in Supplementary file 1q. The observation about ciliary plates in unsorted samples (C146) is evident from Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The speculation about causes (C145) and the conclusion about benefits of unsorted samples (C147) are reasonable inferences from the observations.

results.result: Penetration glands were not captured in the 10X data, possibly due to their large size (20 × 50 µm) and irregular shape. Plate-based scRNA-seq was used for penetration glands to complete the cell-type transcriptome atlas.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C149 explain the methodological approach for gland cells. The absence from 10X data and the use of plate-based scRNA-seq (C149) are clearly described in the methods. The speculation about size and shape (C148) is reasonable given the known dimensions of these cells.

results.result: The two muscle clusters correspond to circular and longitudinal body wall muscles. Differences between these muscle types have been observed in planaria. The expression of Wnt-11-1 and Notum at opposite poles suggests involvement in anterior-posterior axis definition. The unilateral expression of Notum suggests a dorso-ventral and/or left-right axis. Expression of axial patterning genes in muscles suggests they provide positional information to stem cells for patterning of daughter sporocysts.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C157 discuss the muscle populations and their potential roles in patterning. The correspondence to circular and longitudinal muscles (C150) is supported by ISH data. The comparison to planaria (C151) and the role of Wnt signaling in patterning (C152) are supported by citations. The inferences about axis definition (C153-C154) and positional information (C156-C157) are reasonable interpretations of the expression patterns, though they remain hypotheses requiring functional validation.

results.result: The nervous system accounts for over 50% of cells and is the most transcriptionally heterogeneous tissue. At hatching, most miracidia neurons are fully differentiated. Neuron 4 cells resemble bipolar ganglion cells with multi-ciliated nerve endings described by Pan 1980. Their gene expression profile suggests they function as flow and/or vibration sensors. These receptors degenerate 12 hr after transformation to mother sporocyst.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C162 discuss the neural system. The abundance and heterogeneity (C158) are supported by cell counts and clustering data, with citations to similar observations in other animals. The inference about differentiation state (C159) is reasonable from the discrete clustering. The comparison to ultrastructural descriptions (C160, citation to Pan 1980) and functional predictions (C161) are supported by marker expression (polycystins). The degeneration timing (C162) is supported by citation to Poteaux et al. 2023.

results.result: The six submuscular cells expressing ciliary plate markers could play a role in ciliary plate development and function. Their projection into the external environment suggests a sensory role. They could function similarly to ciliomotor pacemaker neurons in Platynereis larvae.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C165 propose functions for the novel submuscular cells. While the expression of ciliary plate markers (C163) is clearly shown, the proposed roles in development/function and sensory function (C163-C164) are inferences from anatomical observations. The comparison to Platynereis (C165, citation provided) is speculative. These are reasonable hypotheses but lack functional validation.

results.result: Ciliary plates are miracidium-specific and shed within 2-48 hr inside the snail. The 16 kDa CaBP is clearly important to ciliary plate function as it is highly expressed in both droplet- and plate-based scRNA-seq. Bulk RNA-seq shows this gene was detected in late embryonic stage, miracidia, and early mother sporocyst.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C169 discuss ciliary plate biology. The stage-specificity (C166) is established knowledge. The shedding timing (C167) is supported by citations. The importance of CaBP (C168) is inferred from high expression across platforms, which is reasonable. The developmental expression pattern (C169) is supported by citations to bulk RNA-seq studies.

results.result: Tegumental cell transcriptomes show a network of genes involved in protein folding, export, and translocation, consistent with ultrastructural observations of abundant RER, ribosomes, and Golgi. RNA velocity analysis revealed dynamic genes crucial in tegument cell maturation across the miracidium to sporocyst transition. Many molecular regulators and markers of adult tegument biogenesis are expressed in miracidia and sporocyst stem and tegument cells, indicating a conserved molecular programme.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C174 discuss tegument cell biology. The STRING analysis results (C170) are shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The consistency with ultrastructure (C171-C172) is supported by citations to Pan 1980 and Meuleman et al. 1978. The RNA velocity findings (C173) are based on Figure 6. The conservation of the tegument developmental programme (C174) is supported by comparison across stages with citations. These are well-supported findings.

results.result: The transcriptomes of the two stem populations suggest they are in different activation states, aligning with the discovery of two stem cell populations in the mother sporocyst with different proliferation kinetics. The pre-activated state of Delta/Phi stem cells may signify they are the first to proliferate after transformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C175-C177 interpret the stem cell states. The different activation states (C175) are inferred from GO analysis (C124-C125). The alignment with sporocyst findings (C176) is supported by citation to Wang et al. 2013. The speculation about proliferation order (C177) is a reasonable hypothesis from the activation state, though it lacks direct evidence.

results.result: The expression of eled and germline-specific regulatory genes in miracidia Kappa cells suggests that cells contributing to the germline may already be segregated at hatching. The presence of spliced-only copies of eled and boule could suggest they are maternal transcripts restricted to primordial germ cells during embryogenesis, though an alternative explanation is that unspliced transcripts are below detection threshold.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C180 propose early germline segregation. The expression of germline markers (C178) is clearly shown, and the inference about segregation is reasonable. However, the interpretation of spliced-only transcripts (C179) is speculative, with an alternative explanation provided (C180). The comparison to zebrafish (C179, citation provided) is suggestive but not definitive. This requires further validation.

results.result: Tissue-specific variation could add a further dimension to dosage compensation in schistosomes. A similar phenomenon has been described in mouse and Drosophila. Sex differences in undifferentiated stem cells have not been reported in later schistosome stages, possibly because earlier studies used older genome versions where sex chromosomes were not well defined. The present study benefited from high coverage and improved genome annotation.
results.evaluation: Claims C183-C187 discuss the novelty and context of the sex-biased findings. The inference about tissue-specific dosage compensation (C183) is supported by the data and citation to Picard et al. 2019. The comparison to other organisms (C184) is supported by citation. The explanation for why this wasn't seen before (C185-C186) is reasonable, supported by citations. The advantages of the current study (C187) are factual.

results.result: The current understanding is that differentiated somatic cells of the miracidium do not continue beyond this stage; stem cells persist and differentiate into subsequent life stages. All miracidium somatic cells are miracidium-only cells. Their transcriptional signatures are similar to comparable tissue types at later stages, suggesting conserved tissue-specific molecular developmental programmes deployed multiple times during the life cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C188-C191 provide context and conclusions. The understanding about somatic cell fate (C188) is supported by citation to Wang et al. 2018. The inference that somatic cells are stage-specific (C189) follows from this. The similarity of transcriptional signatures (C190) is supported by comparisons with citations. The conclusion about conserved programmes (C191) is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: The authors generated single-cell RNA-seq data from miracidia, identifying 19 transcriptionally distinct cell clusters from 20,478 cells that passed quality control. In situ hybridization validated cell type proportions: 93% somatic cells (57% neural, 19% muscle, 13% tegument, 2% parenchyma, 2% protonephridia) and 7% stem cells, with the miracidium composed of approximately 365 cells total.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm the value and quality of this work. Reviewer 1 calls it 'a valuable transcriptomic resource' that is 'beautifully supplemented with in situ hybridization, providing spatial information and absolute cell numbers.' Reviewer 2 notes the study is 'solid' with 'a strength...in its inclusion of in situ hybridisation to validate the predictions of the transcript analysis.' Reviewer 3 states 'the authors validated many of the cluster-defining genes using in situ hybridization chain reaction' and that 'the authors use these markers to count the total number of various cell types in the organism.' No concerns are raised about the clustering, cell counts, or proportions.

results.result: Two muscle clusters were identified based on expression of paramyosin, troponin t, and titin. In situ hybridization identified 74 muscle nuclei (19% of cells), including 28 circular muscle nuclei in two bilaterally symmetrical lines, 33 longitudinal muscle nuclei, and 13 nuclei adjacent to the apical gland. The clusters were distinguished by differential expression of genes including Kunitz-type protease inhibitor (circular muscles), Wnt-11-1 (posterior circular muscles), Notum (anterior muscle cluster), and MyoD (longitudinal muscles).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise the in situ validation work. Reviewer 1 states the work is 'beautifully supplemented with in situ hybridization, providing spatial information and absolute cell numbers.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the authors validated many of the cluster-defining genes using in situ hybridization chain reaction' and 'use these markers to count the total number of various cell types.' No concerns are raised about the muscle characterization or marker validation.

results.result: Five neural clusters were identified expressing markers complexin, prohormone convertase 2, and Smp_068500, accounting for 57% of miracidium cells (209 nuclei). The clusters include diverse neuronal subtypes expressing different neuropeptides (PWamide, Neuropeptide F, Neuropeptide Y, NPP-43, NPP-26), opsins (photoreceptor cells), and mechanosensory markers (polycystins in Neuron 4 cells with multi-ciliated nerve endings). The nervous system is the most transcriptionally heterogeneous tissue in the miracidium.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the quality of the cell type characterization. Reviewer 1 describes the work as providing 'spatial information and absolute cell numbers for many of the recovered transcriptomic states.' Reviewer 3 notes the validation of 'cluster-defining genes using in situ hybridization chain reaction' and that 'the authors use these markers to count the total number of various cell types.' No concerns are raised about the neural characterization or diversity.

results.result: Penetration gland cells were not captured in the 10X droplet-based data, possibly due to their large size and irregular shape. The authors used plate-based single-cell RNA-seq on 37 manually selected gland cells to complete the cell-type atlas. These cells showed co-expression of neural and muscle markers and expressed five venom antigen-like (VAL) genes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly praises this methodological approach: 'Because the authors realized that their cell isolation protocols were biasing the cell types they were sequencing, they applied a second method to help them recover additional cell types.' This demonstrates reviewer acceptance of both the problem identification and the solution. No concerns are raised about this approach.

results.result: A small cluster of 40 ciliary plate cells was identified based on expression of 16-kDa calcium-binding protein and p25 alpha. These markers were also expressed in six previously undescribed submuscular cells with projections to the exterior. The ciliary plate cluster was only found in sufficient numbers in unsorted samples, demonstrating the benefit of including unsorted cells to capture fragile or unusually shaped cell types.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly affirms this finding and approach: 'Because the authors realized that their cell isolation protocols were biasing the cell types they were sequencing, they applied a second method to help them recover additional cell types.' The discovery of the submuscular cells and the methodological insight about unsorted samples are implicitly accepted through the overall positive assessment. No concerns are raised.

results.result: A tegument cluster of 366 cells was identified based on expression of adult tegument markers including dynein light chain, DUF3421 domain protein, and MEG6. In situ hybridization showed 46 Meg6-positive cells with nuclei below the body wall muscle and cytoplasmic protrusions forming epidermal ridges. The tegument transcriptome shows genes involved in protein folding, export, and translocation, consistent with ultrastructural observations of abundant RER, ribosomes, and Golgi apparatus.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the quality of cell type characterization and validation. Reviewer 1 notes the work provides 'spatial information and absolute cell numbers for many of the recovered transcriptomic states.' Reviewer 3 states 'the authors validated many of the cluster-defining genes using in situ hybridization chain reaction.' No concerns are raised about the tegument characterization.

results.result: A protonephridial cluster of 536 cells was identified expressing genes common to excretory systems (nephrin, odd-skipped-related) and the protonephridia marker Smp_335600. In situ hybridization showed expression around six nuclei in a bilaterally symmetrical pattern, with transcripts distributed along s-shaped excretory tubules connecting anterior and posterior flame cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the validation approach. Reviewer 1 states the work provides 'spatial information and absolute cell numbers for many of the recovered transcriptomic states.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the authors validated many of the cluster-defining genes using in situ hybridization chain reaction.' No concerns are raised about the protonephridia characterization.

results.result: Two parenchyma clusters (1093 and 605 cells) were identified expressing markers similar to later developmental stages (hypothetical protein Smp_063330, cathepsin B-like cysteine proteinase, serpin). The zinc transporter Slc39a7 was a top marker, with in situ expression in 7-9 cells showing long cytoplasmic protrusions filling intercellular space.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the validation work. Reviewer 1 notes the work provides 'spatial information and absolute cell numbers for many of the recovered transcriptomic states.' Reviewer 3 states 'the authors validated many of the cluster-defining genes using in situ hybridization chain reaction.' No concerns are raised about the parenchyma characterization.

results.result: Seven stem cell clusters (10,686 cells) were identified based on expression of known markers (ago2-1, nanos-2, fgfrA, fgfrB, klf, hesl). These resolved into two main populations: Delta/Phi-like (Stems C and D, expressing p53-1) and Kappa-like (Stems A and B, expressing UPPA). In situ hybridization showed 20-29 Ago2-1+ cells (median 23, ~7% of larva), with 12-14 p53-1+ cells and 8-9 UPPA+ cells. The two populations are distinguished by sex-linked gene expression, collapsing into single clusters when sex chromosome genes are removed.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 calls 'the identification of sex-specific transcriptomic states within the populations of stem cells...particularly unexpected.' Reviewer 3 states 'Schistosomes have ZW sex chromosomes and the authors make the interesting observation that the stem cells at this stage are already expressing sex (i.e. W)-specific genes.' The validation with in situ hybridization is praised by all reviewers. No concerns are raised.

results.result: Each of the two main stem cell populations shows sex-biased transcriptional signatures, with the Delta/Phi and Kappa clusters separating based on sex-linked gene expression. This suggests incomplete gene dosage compensation in the miracidium with tissue-specific variation, as sex-biased clustering is observed in stem cells but not in somatic cell clusters.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this as an important finding. Reviewer 1 calls 'the identification of sex-specific transcriptomic states within the populations of stem cells...particularly unexpected.' Reviewer 3 states this is 'the interesting observation that the stem cells at this stage are already expressing sex (i.e. W)-specific genes.' The interpretation about dosage compensation is not challenged. No concerns are raised.

results.result: DNA replication does not occur in miracidium stem or somatic cells during the free-swimming stage, as shown by lack of EdU incorporation. Since stem cells start proliferating in the mother sporocyst approximately 20 hours post-infection, both stem cell populations pause cell division for at least 26 hours.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about this finding. The overall positive assessment of the methods and data by all three reviewers, with Reviewer 2 noting the study is 'solid' and Reviewer 3 stating 'the methods, data and analyses broadly support the claims with only minor weaknesses,' indicates acceptance of this result. No specific critiques are mentioned.

results.result: The two stem populations show different activation states based on their transcriptomes. Delta/Phi cells are enriched for ribosomal proteins and translation-related genes (markers of pre-activation) and express six transcription factors (lin-39, tiptop, hes-related, p53-1, Zfp-1, six-3-1) indicating a multipotent progenitor stage. Kappa cells are enriched for genes involved in transcription, metabolism, glycolysis, and lipid metabolism, indicating a quiescent state.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these interpretations. The overall positive assessment by all reviewers, with Reviewer 3 stating 'the methods, data and analyses broadly support the claims with only minor weaknesses,' indicates acceptance. The differential gene expression analysis and GO analysis supporting these conclusions are not questioned.

results.result: The Delta/Phi stem population is the origin of the tegument lineage, as shown by co-expression of three tegument-specific transcription factors (p53-1, zfp-1, six3-1). RNA velocity analysis indicates progression from Delta/Phi stem cells toward miracidia tegument cells, with high-speed differentiation to sporocyst tegument. The analysis revealed dynamic genes (p53-1, zfp-1) crucial for tegument maturation across the life cycle transition. Many molecular regulators of adult tegument biogenesis are expressed in miracidia stem and tegument cells, indicating a conserved developmental program.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about this trajectory analysis or interpretation. The overall positive assessment by all reviewers indicates acceptance. Reviewer 3 states 'the methods, data and analyses broadly support the claims with only minor weaknesses,' and no specific critiques of the RNA velocity analysis or lineage conclusions are mentioned.

results.result: The Kappa stem population likely contains pluripotent cells that will contribute to cercariae development and the germline, based on expression of germline-specific genes (p53-2, eled, onecut1, irx, akkn, boule). The finding that eled and germline regulatory genes are expressed in miracidia Kappa cells suggests germline cells may already be segregated at hatching. The presence of spliced-only copies of eled and boule could suggest they are maternal transcripts restricted to primordial germ cells during embryogenesis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these interpretations about germline identity. The overall positive assessment by all reviewers indicates acceptance. Reviewer 3 states 'the methods, data and analyses broadly support the claims with only minor weaknesses,' and no specific concerns about the germline conclusions are raised. The speculation about maternal transcripts is presented as a possibility, not a definitive claim.

results.result: Some cell types were preferentially recovered in the scRNA-seq data. Stem cells comprised only 7% of total cells by in situ counts but accounted for ~52% of scRNA-seq data. Ciliary plates were only found in sufficient numbers in unsorted samples. This demonstrates benefits of including unsorted samples to discover cell type diversity, especially for fragile, sticky, or unusually shaped cells, though preferential recovery may be due to differences in robustness to dissociation, sorting, and/or microfluidics.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly praises this methodological insight: 'Because the authors realized that their cell isolation protocols were biasing the cell types they were sequencing, they applied a second method to help them recover additional cell types.' This demonstrates clear reviewer acceptance of both the problem identification and the solution. No concerns are raised about this observation or interpretation.

results.result: Expression of Wnt-11-1 and Notum in circular muscles at opposite poles suggests these muscles define the anterior-posterior axis. The unilateral, asymmetrical expression of Notum at the anterior end suggests a dorso-ventral and/or left-right axis not previously identified in miracidia. Expression of axial patterning gene orthologues in muscles suggests they may regulate stem cells during homeostasis in adults and provide positional information to mother sporocyst stem cells for axial patterning of daughter sporocysts.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these interpretations about axial patterning. The overall positive assessment by all reviewers indicates acceptance. Reviewer 3 states 'the methods, data and analyses broadly support the claims with only minor weaknesses,' and no specific concerns about these conclusions are raised.

results.result: The miracidium, with its diversity of differentiated cells in relatively low numbers (~365 cells), makes a simple and tractable system for understanding schistosome cell biology. Current understanding is that differentiated somatic cells do not continue beyond the miracidium stage—they are miracidium-only cells—while stem cells persist and differentiate into subsequent life stages. However, transcriptional signatures of miracidium somatic cells are similar to comparable tissue types at later stages, suggesting conserved tissue-specific molecular developmental programs deployed multiple times during the life cycle.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the value of this resource and these conclusions. Reviewer 1 calls it 'a valuable transcriptomic resource' and 'a rich resource to complement the biology of this complex system.' Reviewer 2 states it is 'a valuable study' that provides 'an expression profile.' Reviewer 3 notes 'this study adds to the growing single-cell resources' and is 'a useful resource for the field.' The interpretations about conserved programs are not challenged.
